title: More than 60 years after it was redone, the feud over the Paris Opera's ceiling isn't over
subhead: In 1960, French Culture Minister André Malraux commissioned a painting from artist Marc Chagall to modernize the ceiling of the Opéra Garnier, thereby concealing the 19th-century work of Jules-Eugène Lenepveu. The controversial decision reflected a battle between two visions of cultural heritage, and today, one of Lenepveu's descendants is determined to restore his ancestor's creation.

subhead: 'Aquatic Monuments' (6/6). The Saint-Georges pool, located just steps from Rennes' city center, opened in 1926 on the site of a former church. Listed as a historic monument since 2016, this Art Deco building adorned with mosaics is a source of pride for residents.

title: Navigating the Suez Canal demands technical skills costing hundreds of thousands of dollars
subhead: 'Suez, a historic canal' (5/6). The waterway connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea is a vital artery for global trade. To travel through it, vessels must comply with strict regulations and pay transit fees that can reach nearly $1 million.

title: How Céline Dion became the queen of Vegas (and is about to set Paris alight)
subhead: It was in Las Vegas that the Canadian superstar prepared the series of shows she will perform in Paris starting in September. She lived in Sin City for more than 20 years and reached the height of her career by reinventing the concept of a residency.

title: The hunt for musketeer d'Artagnan's tomb sparks archaeological row
subhead: Archaeologist Wim Dijkman uncovered a skeleton in a church in the Netherlands that could belong to the famous French musketeer. The municipality accused him of carrying out illegal excavations and took the project away from him. It will take a few more months before the DNA analysis reveals its secrets.

title: Egypt turned the Suez Canal from a symbol of exploitation into a tool for emancipation
subhead: 'Suez, a historic canal' (4/6). The air along the maritime route has long carried a whiff of rebellion. It was an uprising in Ismailia, one of the canal's cities, that led to the founding of the Egyptian Republic in 1952, ending a monarchy subservient to London. By nationalizing the waterway in 1956, and defending it against French, British and Israeli attacks, the country established its international legitimacy.
